messages.subject: [statnet_help] transitive triples
messages.body_plain:
I am new to Statnet and I am trying to compare the % of transitive triples (called the weighted overall graph clustering coefficient in UCINET) across my observed (undirected) network and a set of simulated networks. Is this possible? I have used the command gof to compare distance, degree, etc. but I can't seem to figure out how to compare transitivity.

Thanks,
Tait

messages.subject: [statnet_help] transitive triples
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tait,

As you know, the gof command automates the comparison of network 
statistics from an original network to a set of simulated networks.  In 
the process it compiles the statistic across all the runs, calcuates a 
p-value, and creates plots.  Gof is only implemented for a short list of 
network statistics; however, the steps involved are straigthforward, and 
can easily be implemented by the interested user for any other network 
statistic of interest, either by adding code to their copy of gof, or by 
writing a few new lines of independent code. Reading through the gof code 
is a good way to see examples of the syntax one might use for this. We 
also have an example doing this for triangles in Section 8 of the statnet 
tutorial paper.

http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i09/paper

In terms of calculating your statistic of interest on any given network, 
you may be able to use a function within sna or ergm if it exists, or else 
you'll have to write it.

Yours,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] sna, large networks, and the network data structure
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] sna, large networks, and the network data structure
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm working on a project the requires generating social network
metrics on a graph with a set of vertices on the order of 10^5 to 10^6
nodes. I'm able to represent the network using the "network" data
structure from the network package, but when I try to run sna
functions on my network, I get the following error:

Error in matrix(0, nr = network.size(x), nc = network.size(x)) :
  too many elements specified

The reason is that R is only able to create matrices with 2^31-1
because a matrix is really a vector with a dim attribute, and this
vector is indexed by a signed integer (this property is independent of
system architecture -- running on a 64-bit system will not help).
Since all of the sna functions start by coercing whatever data type
it's handed (including the network data type) into a full matrix, this
puts a hard limit on the size of graphs that sna can analyze at 46,340
vertices.

It seems like the network package was developed specifically to keep
this type of thing from happening. The network C API gives all of the
necessary power to construct all the measures that are currently
inefficiently calculated in sna. Have the sna developers considered
overhauling sna to use the network data structure as the primary data
structue instead of the sociomatrix?

I've started to modify the underlying C code to use the network API so
that I can run some of the analyses that I need on graphs with
millions of nodes, and I've had a lot of success. I would be happy to
contribute the work that I've done to the sna project, but want to
make sure that I'm not duplicating effort. Who can I talk to to start
contributing?

Thanks,
Alex D'Amour
Statistical Programmer
Harvard Institute for Quantitative Social Science

Hi, Alex -

Alex D'Amour wrote:
> Hello all,
> 
> I'm working on a project the requires generating social network
> metrics on a graph with a set of vertices on the order of 10^5 to 10^6
> nodes. I'm able to represent the network using the "network" data

> because a matrix is really a vector with a dim attribute, and this
> vector is indexed by a signed integer (this property is independent of

> Since all of the sna functions start by coercing whatever data type

> vertices.
> 
> It seems like the network package was developed specifically to keep
> this type of thing from happening. The network C API gives all of the
> necessary power to construct all the measures that are currently
> inefficiently calculated in sna. Have the sna developers considered
> overhauling sna to use the network data structure as the primary data
> structue instead of the sociomatrix?
> 
> I've started to modify the underlying C code to use the network API so
> that I can run some of the analyses that I need on graphs with
> millions of nodes, and I've had a lot of success. I would be happy to
> contribute the work that I've done to the sna project, but want to
> make sure that I'm not duplicating effort. Who can I talk to to start
> contributing?

What you are running into is the grand old phenomenon of "legacy code." 
  When sna was first being accumulated in the late 1990s, a "large" 
social network data set had 50-100 nodes.  Sparse-graph performance was 
a not a major issue at that time, nor was support for truly huge graphs. 
  For the most part, this is still the case: despite the "bigger is 
better" push of recent years, most social network data sets are still no 
more than 1-2k nodes, and are handled just fine by adjacency matrices.

That said, an important and growing body of users have much larger data 
sets, and supporting those is also a goal.  As you note, this was one of 
the factors behind the development of the network package, and has been 
considered to a greater or lesser degree in other modern statnet 
components.  The issue, then, is with migrating the old (but useful) 
routines to support the new data structures.

The first step in this process (taken a while back) was to make sure 
that sna and network were functionally interoperable, in the basic sense 
that calling an sna routine with a network object should yield 
reasonable results.  To get to this first milestone, we simply used the 
expedient of transparently coercing network objects (and other 
reasonable data) to adjacency form, and passing this to the existing 
code.  This works, but obviously does not convey any of the other 
advantages of the network package to sna -- in particular, none of the 
scalability advantages apply.

What I've been working on recently is "phase two" of the transition. 
This involves:

   1. Introducing a new interim edgelist standard, which is simple 
enough not to require additional package support (e.g., network), but 
which keeps the scalability/sparsity advantages.
   2. Modifying the internal coercion routines to recognize and use this 
format, and introducing a new (internal) coercion routine to efficiently 
convert existing sparse data objects (network objects and SparseM 
matrices) thereto.
   3. Gradually converting extant routines to natively and transparently 
employ edgelists where feasible.

Although I could use the network API for this purpose, I elected to take 
this route as the interim solution to a full network-based migration. 
This is for three reasons: first, sna has historically been a standalone 
option, and I am inclined to keep that possibility for the time being; 
second, the development path is easier with the interim step (which can 
be more quickly rolled out than a full makeover); and third, there are 
various ways in which the interim step will facilitate the final 
migration to native network object support.  I won't go into all the 
details here, but it basically boils down to the fact that sna is a big 
and fairly stable package, and I can't pull the rug out from under it. 
Luckily, that's not necessary to give folks most of what they want (at 
least, in increments)!

Since this is rapidly getting into a deeper development discussion, I 
don't want to spam the list with too much more of it.  However, if 
you're interested in helping out, that would be great -- the primary 
limitation on progress right now is my own time, which is sliced very 
thinly these days.  (I'm also working on some further updates to 
network, including enhanced dynamic data support, so there are lots of 
irons in the fire!)  I need to get the current development version of 
sna somewhat more stabilized, but at that point I should be in a 
position to highlight specific code contributions which would be 
especially welcome.  I am targeting mid-March for the next release, in 
part since I want to use the updated version in my Spring methods class. 
  :-)

For those of you who are reading this with confusion and trepidation 
(or, alternately, hope and excitement), let me add a few observations 
about the new version:

1. It will not break any existing code.  Your current sna-based scripts 
should work just fine.
2. The new edgelist form will be a new "low-tech" option for those who 
want it, but will not be mandatory.  (Objects like networks and SparseM 
matrices will be automagically handled, as before, but now without 
adjacency matrix conversion in most cases.)
3. Not every routine will immediately see efficiency gains from this 
process, although several have been targeted for the initial update.  As 
routines are re-written, various things will suddenly run much faster 
and/or with much less memory for large, sparse graphs.
4. Users working with ordinary-scale data won't notice much of a change. 
  (But the new release does have some new functions and other goodies 
that may be of interest.)

Hopefully this gives an initial cut at the answers to your questions. 
Volunteers for the conversion effort should contact me directly, and 
I'll send out some additional information over the next few days.

Thanks!

-Carter
